specPoints.text: be able to use energy cycles and energy level diagrams to calculate the enthalpy change of solution of an ionic compound, using enthalpy change of hydration and lattice energy

be able to use entropy and enthalpy changes of solution values to predict the solubility of ionic compounds and discuss trends in the solubility of ionic compounds covered in Unit 2 Further suggested practical Calculate the enthalpy change when a variety of ionic solids are dissolved in water

primer.text: One energy cycle links the three quantities every solution calculation turns on: lattice enthalpy, enthalpy of solution and the hydration enthalpies of both ions. This note constructs the cycle for potassium chloride and magnesium chloride, extracts an unknown hydration enthalpy by Hess's law, and explains solubility through total entropy.

lessons.title: One cycle, three enthalpies
lessons.opening: One energy cycle links everything solution calculations ask for. Gaseous ions can reach aqueous solution directly (hydration) or indirectly (lattice first, then dissolution), and Hess's law equates the routes. Add the two ions' hydration terms together, and any missing value falls out - chloride at -363 for KCl, magnesium at -1921 for MgCl2.
keyPoints: Solution calculations supply lattice enthalpy, enthalpy of solution and one ion's hydration enthalpy, asking for the other ion's hydration enthalpy.

Route 1 runs gaseous ions to ionic solid (reverse lattice) to aqueous ions (solution); Route 2 runs gaseous ions straight to aqueous ions (hydration); Hess's law equates the routes, giving delta hyd H (total) = delta latt H + delta sol H.
Each ion carries its own hydration enthalpy, and the total is the sum of the anion's and cation's terms.
For KCl: delta hyd H[Cl-] = (-711) + (+26) - (-322) = -363 kJ mol^-1.
MgCl2: delta hyd H[Mg2+] = -2592 - 55 + 726 = -1921 kJ mol^-1.
A Born-Haber style energy level diagram is an equally valid route, as long as labels and arrow directions match the definitions.

low.restatement: Hydration total = lattice + solution; subtract the known ion's term to isolate the unknown; KCl: -711 + 26 + 322 = -363.
low.analogy: Two roads to the same town: the direct motorway (hydration) equals the toll road plus the side street (lattice then solution).
low.examPointer: Watch doubled terms - MgCl2 subtracts two chloride hydration values, not one.

medium.restatement: The cycle is a two-door room: gaseous ions leave by the direct hydration door or by the lattice-then-dissolution corridor; Hess's law pins both doors' totals equal.
medium.analogy: Reaching a rooftop by lift (direct) or stairs and ladder (indirect) - same altitude change.
medium.examPointer: Draw the cycle before any arithmetic; mislabelled arrows are the top error source.

Explain why the two ions' hydration enthalpies must both appear in the cycle.
check.modelAnswer: Dissolving one formula unit hydrates every ion it contains, so the total hydration term is the sum over all ions; an unknown for one ion is isolated only after the partner's term is accounted for.

check.stem: A sodium chloride cycle gives delta latt H = -787, delta sol H = +4 and delta hyd H[Cl-] = -384 kJ mol^-1. Find delta hyd H[Na+].
check.modelAnswer: Total hydration = -787 + 4 = -783; sodium's share = -783 - (-384) = -399 kJ mol^-1.

lessons.title: Predicting solubility from entropy
lessons.opening: Why do some salts dissolve and others not? The answer rides on total entropy: dissolving raises the system's entropy as the lattice disperses, but the surroundings' term equals minus the solution enthalpy over temperature. Ammonium nitrate at 298 K shows the arithmetic: +108.7 system, -86.6 surroundings, +22.1 total - soluble, with a tiny activation energy clearing the way.
keyPoints: Dissolving breaks the lattice (endothermic, and disorder rises as particles multiply) while hydration orders the surrounding water (exothermic, lowering water's entropy).
Solubility therefore depends on the entropy of the system, the enthalpy of solution, and the temperature of the water.
Delta S total = delta S system - delta sol H / T combines the two books.
Ammonium nitrate at 298 K: delta sol H = +25.8 kJ mol^-1; delta S system works out from 113.4 plus 146.4 minus 151.1 as +108.7 J K^-1 mol^-1.
Delta S surroundings: -25800 divided by 298 gives -86.6 J K^-1 mol^-1; delta S total: 108.7 minus 86.6, making +22.1 J K^-1 mol^-1, spontaneous, hence soluble.
The activation energy for the process is very low, so at 298 K ammonium nitrate dissolves readily.

low.restatement: Delta S total = delta S system - delta sol H / T; a positive total means soluble; ammonium nitrate's +108.7 versus -86.6 leaves +22.1.
low.analogy: A crowd dispersing (system up) while the ushers tidy rows (surroundings down): the day succeeds if the dispersal wins.
low.examPointer: Convert the solution enthalpy to joules before dividing by T - the /1000 slip strikes again.

medium.restatement: Two entropies tug against each other on dissolving: the ions gain freedom while the hydration shell's water loses it, and the enthalpy term prices the surroundings' share.
medium.analogy: A park opening its gates (people spread) while gardeners trim hedges (order imposed): success depends on which change is bigger.
medium.examPointer: End the answer with the feasibility verdict and the low-Ea remark.

check.modelAnswer: The entropy of the system, the enthalpy change of solution, and the temperature of the water in kelvin.

check.stem: Explain why an endothermic dissolving can still be spontaneous.
check.modelAnswer: The system's entropy rise from dispersing the lattice can exceed the surroundings' entropy cost of supplying the enthalpy; when the total is positive, the second law permits the change despite the cooling flask.

check.stem: A salt has delta sol H = +40 kJ mol^-1 and delta S system = +150 J K^-1 mol^-1. Is it soluble at 298 K?
check.modelAnswer: Delta S surroundings = -40000/298 = -134.2 J K^-1 mol^-1, so delta S total = 150 - 134.2 = +15.8 J K^-1 mol^-1: positive, so the salt dissolves at 298 K.

workedExample.prompt: Work out the chloride ion's enthalpy of hydration, given delta latt H [KCl] = -711, delta sol H [KCl] = +26 and delta hyd H [K+] = -322, all in kJ mol^-1.
steps: Draw the energy cycle with delta hyd H[Cl-] as the unknown.
Write the Hess's law balance: total hydration = lattice + solution, so delta hyd H[K+] + delta hyd H[Cl-] = (-711) + (+26).
Substitute the potassium term: delta hyd H[Cl-] = (-711) + (+26) - (-322).
